candidate_sources.title: Cercospora longipes (brown leaf spot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive CABI Compendium datasheet covering Identity, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected, and Further Information on Cercospora longipes, the causal agent of brown spot in sugarcane

candidate_sources.title: Brown spot of sugarcane: an emerging disease in South Western region in India
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research on brown spot of sugarcane as an emerging disease in South Western India, with documentation of severe outbreaks caused by Cercospora longipes in Karnataka and Maharashtra regions

candidate_sources.title: Field Crops: Sugarcane | LSU AgCenter
candidate_sources.snippet: LSU AgCenter management guide for sugarcane field crops diseases, providing extension recommendations for disease identification and management strategies

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane grassy shoot phytoplasma (grassy shoot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet covering identity, overview, distribution, dispersal, hosts, vectors, diagnosis, biology, ecology, environmental requirements, impacts, and prevention/control. Characteristic symptoms include chlorotic-white, creamy or green leaves and premature proliferation of lateral buds forming numerous lanky tillers with severe stunting, giving a typical grassy appearance. Caused by sugarcane grassy shoot (SCGS) phytoplasma belonging to Rice Yellow Dwarf group (16SrXI). Causes 5-70% yield reduction in plant crop and up to 100% in ratoon crops.

candidate_sources.title: Molecular and Symptom Analysis Reveal the Presence of New Phytoplasmas Associated with Sugarcane Grassy Shoot Disease in India | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research in Plant Disease journal from American Phytopathological Society examining molecular and symptom characteristics of new phytoplasmas associated with sugarcane grassy shoot disease in India. Phytoplasma-infected sugarcane plants show proliferation of tillers giving typical grassy appearance with white or creamy yellow leaves. Phytoplasmas are small, pleomorphic, pathogenic mycoplasma (class Mollicutes) causing yield losses from 5-20% in sugarcane, up to 100% loss in ratoon crops.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: GRASSY SHOOT
candidate_sources.snippet: Educational resource covering major sugarcane disease. Grassy shoot is caused by Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari. Symptoms include whitening or yellowing of leaves, shortening of internodes leading to stunted growth, smaller leaves, and excessive proliferation of shoots resulting in broom phenotype. Transmitted by phloem-feeding leafhopper vectors (Saccharosydne saccharivora, Matsumuratettix hiroglyphicus, Deltocephalus vulgaris, Yamatotettix flavovittatus) and seed material in this vegetatively propagated crop.

candidate_sources.title: SS-AGR-201/SC001: Sugarcane Leaf Scald
candidate_sources.snippet: Sugarcane Leaf Scald is a bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. Symptoms include white pencil lines (1-2 mm wide) on leaves extending from midrib to margin with diffuse yellow borders. As disease progresses, brown necrotic tissue develops from leaf tip or margin, and leaves curl inward giving a scalded appearance. Susceptible varieties show yield losses exceeding 40% and 30% reduction in juice quality. Management includes using resistant varieties and planting disease-free cuttings.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Diseases: Gummosis and Leaf Scald | Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
candidate_sources.snippet: USDA APHIS provides information on sugarcane diseases including Gummosis and Leaf Scald. Leaf Scald is a significant bacterial disease affecting sugarcane production. The pathogen causes characteristic leaf symptoms and can result in latent infections where plants show no external symptoms while still harboring the bacterium.

candidate_sources.title: Recent Advances in Sugarcane Leaf Scald Disease: Pathogenic Insights and Sustainable Management Approaches
candidate_sources.snippet: This peer-reviewed article reviews recent advances in understanding sugarcane Leaf Scald disease caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. It covers pathogenic mechanisms, molecular biology, defense responses of sugarcane genotypes, and sustainable management approaches including genetic resistance and disease-free planting material.

candidate_sources.title: Pokkah Boeng - Disease of Sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Pokkah boeng is caused by Fusarium species. Symptoms include red streaking, chlorosis, necrosis, twisted and deformed leaves, and the characteristic 'knife-cut' appearance with ladder-like internal lesions. The disease spreads primarily by airborne spores, with secondary transmission via infected setts, irrigation water, and soil. Management involves cultivating resistant varieties, removing affected canes, and applying fungicides like carbendazim, copper oxychloride, or mancozeb.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Pokkah Boeng Disease: Insights and Future Directions for Effective Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of Pokkah Boeng disease caused by multiple Fusarium species including F. verticillioides, F. fujikuroi, F. sacchari, F. oxysporum, and F. proliferatum. Symptoms include yellowing of spindle leaves, red stripes, twisted deformed young leaves, chlorotic leaf sheaths, and brown or pink internal discoloration. Control strategies include resistant variety selection, cultural practices, fungicide applications, and emerging biocontrol agents such as Trichoderma species.

candidate_sources.title: Genetic Diversity and Pathogenicity of Fusarium fujikuroi Species Complex (FFSC) Causing Sugarcane Pokkah Boeng Disease (PBD) in China
candidate_sources.snippet: APS publication documenting genetic diversity of Fusarium fujikuroi species complex causing Pokkah Boeng disease. Details pathogenicity assessments of major FFSC species including F. fujikuroi, F. sacchari, F. oxysporum, F. verticillioides, and F. proliferatum. Discusses symptom development including yellowing, twisting of spindle, red stripes, necrotic spots, and top rot phenotypes under field conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Surveying Potential Soilborne Pathogens Causing Sett Rot on Sugarcane in Southern Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Surveys conducted during the 2023 and 2024 planting seasons identified Thielaviopsis sp. and Fusarium sp. in 43 and 38% of 569 sampled seed cane, respectively. Evidence indicates that sett rot-causing pathogens are soil-borne fungi that attack seed pieces during germination, leading to significant crop losses through reduced stand establishment.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: SETT ROT OR PINEAPPLE DISEASE
candidate_sources.snippet: Affected tissues first develop a reddish colour which turns to brownish black in the later stages. The severely affected setts show internodal cavities covered with the mycelium and abundant spores. A characteristic pineapple smell is associated with the rotting tissues. Setts can be treated in hot water at 51°C for 30 minutes.

candidate_sources.title: Glomerella tucumanensis (red rot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Glomerella tucumanensis attacks sugarcane setts in the soil causing them to rot as they germinate, and standing cane in the field causing diseased canes to wilt and shrivel. The fungus is one of several pathogens causing sett-borne diseases in sugarcane, with significant impacts on stand establishment.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane pineapple disease (218)
candidate_sources.snippet: Pineapple disease (also called sett rot) is caused by Ceratocystis paradoxa and primarily affects the setts usually two to three weeks after planting. The fungus is soil-borne and enters through cut ends and proliferates rapidly in the parenchymatous tissues. Roots fail to form, buds fail to grow, and those that do remain stunted or die back.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane streak mosaic virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: The CABI Compendium datasheet on Sugarcane streak mosaic virus covers Impact, Identity, Overview, Associated Diseases, Pests or Pathogens, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Environmental Requirements, Seedborne Aspects, Natural Enemies, Impacts, Prevention/Control and Further Information.

candidate_sources.title: Historical Review of Sugarcane Streak Mosaic Virus that Has Recently Emerged in Africa | Phytopathology®
candidate_sources.snippet: Sugarcane streak mosaic virus (SCSMV), now assigned to the genus Poacevirus of the family Potyviridae, was reported for the first time in 1932 in Louisiana. The symptoms of SCSMV-infected sugarcane include leaf color fading, uneven leaf size, irregular mosaic, mottles, and streaks on leaves. Geographic distribution includes most Asian countries such as Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Iran, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Vietnam, and China, with recent emergence in Africa.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Sugarcane Streak Mosaic Virus Infecting Sugarcane in Côte d'Ivoire | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: First documentation of natural infection of sugarcane by SCSMV in Africa occurred in Côte d'Ivoire. The disease causes irregular yellow and green mosaic, interveinal chlorotic specks, and streaks on leaves. SCSMV can affect several yield parameters such as stalk weight, diameter, and sugar content, with documented yield reductions when infection levels exceed 50%.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Disease: Characteristics, Identification and Control | MDPI
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed article covering characteristics, identification methods, and control measures for sugarcane mosaic diseases. Discusses pathogenicity and genetic diversity of multiple viruses including SCSMV, SCMV, and SCBV. SCSMV genome is 9.8 kilo-nucleotides containing positive-sense single-stranded RNA encoding a large polyprotein with 10 mature proteins.

candidate_sources.title: PP313/PP313: Mosaic Disease of St. Augustinegrass Caused by Sugarcane Mosaic Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension publication documenting mosaic disease of St. Augustinegrass caused by Sugarcane Mosaic Virus (SCMV), including symptom descriptions, transmission methods, and management recommendations. Symptoms include broken yellow streaks between veins with chlorotic or yellowish stripes alternating with normal green leaf portions. Transmission occurs via mechanical means and aphids. Management includes plant host resistance and equipment sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Disease: Characteristics, Identification and Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed scientific article examining characteristics, identification methods, and control measures for Sugarcane Mosaic Disease. Covers the pathogenic virus of family Potyviridae, symptom manifestation including mosaic-like patterns of light and dark green on leaves, necrosis in severe infections with yield loss, and resistance-based management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Virus - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
candidate_sources.snippet: Academic overview of Sugarcane Mosaic Virus (SCMV) covering pathogen information, symptomatology, epidemiology, and management approaches for sugarcane cultivation. Provides comprehensive discussion of virus characteristics and control strategies in agricultural contexts.

candidate_sources.title: SS-AGR-256 Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet from University of Florida describing symptoms including yellowing of midribs and leaf clustering, pathogen identification as Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) transmitted by aphids, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Present Status and Future Management Strategies for Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus: A Major Constraint to the Global Sugarcane Production
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed article detailing the global impact of Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV), symptom expression including midrib yellowing and necrosis, the Luteoviridae family pathogen, and evidence-based management strategies for disease control.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Virus and Phytoplasma Pathogens Associated with Yellow Leaf Syndrome of Sugarcane in Cuba
candidate_sources.snippet: APS journal publication reporting the identification of viral and phytoplasma pathogens associated with yellow leaf syndrome in sugarcane cultivars, with diagnostic and symptom information for this economically important disease.

candidate_sources.title: Plant Pathology Circular No. 289 - Florida Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellow spot initially appears as small 1-2mm diameter yellow lesions on leaves, mostly on the younger foliage. As the lesions enlarge under favorable weather conditions, the spots can reach 1-2cm across and are generally irregular and elongated along the leaf axis. Red pigmentation develops around and in lesions as the infected leaves mature.

candidate_sources.title: Identification of a major quantitative trait locus (QTL) for yellow spot (Mycovellosiella koepkei) disease resistance in sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellow spot is a foliar disease of sugarcane caused by Mycovellosiella koepkei (Kruger) Deighton. Fungicides such as benomyl, basic copper sulfate, copper oxychloride, and sulfur dust can be used to control yellow spot, but resistant varieties provide the basis for control. Breakdown of host resistance has been noted in Australia and Mauritius.

candidate_sources.title: Molecular characterisation of Mycovellosiella koepki, the causal agent of yellow spot disease of sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Mycovellosiella koepkei is found almost exclusively on Saccharum officinarum Linn. AFLP and microsatellite (SSR) markers have been used to identify genetic variation in the pathogen. The pathogen exhibits complex epidemiology with impacts on sugarcane production in multiple regions.
